parsedVerdict.reasoning: Most of ReserveSpotService is what an application-layer use case should do. It goes through injected ports (SpotRepository, ReservationRepository, PaymentPort), hands the clash check and pricing to domain objects (r.clashesWith, spot.priceFor), and returns a plain receipt. The problem is the use-case method `reserve(plate, from, hours, electric, request?: Request)`. It takes an Express HTTP `Request` as a parameter. That puts a transport/framework type into the application use case, and handling HTTP requests is a presentation-layer job (adapters-inbound). Whether the file may import 'express' at all is an import-direction question and out of scope here. What is in scope is that the use case's own signature is tied to the HTTP transport, so the application layer now carries a presentation concern. The parameter is never used inside the method, but the contract still ties every caller to Express. A smaller point: the 1–24 hour limit on reservations is a business rule that would fit better as an invariant on the Reservation domain model. Input validation in an application service is still defensible, so the main finding is the transport coupling.
